July the 21. the army all im barct to Set out for tiantorogo

citations.analysis_notes: Six independent bibliographic, statutory, toponymic, authorial, and lexical proofs falsify the 'c. 1798' baseline date: (1) Bibliographic: Zero 1798 imprints titled Band of Brothers exist in Evans's American Bibliography (1639–1800), Sabin, or OCLC; the work was first serialized by J. H. Green in Cincinnati's The Casket (July 1 – Sept. 16, 1846, CERT-3300-202) without Chapter XII and first published in book form by G. B. Zieber & Co. in Philadelphia in spring 1847 (CERT-3300-203, CERT-3300-204). (p. 123, CERT-3300-204) he defines the exact same pair ('Coney' / 'Bogus') in his own 1847 authorial footnotes. (4) Toponymic anachronism on p. 122: Letter No. 3, dated 'October 20, 1825', names 'Manhattan, Ohio', a speculative Maumee River port town not platted until 1835. citations.verbatim_quote: Bogus (bōu·gəs), (sb.1) a. [A cant word of U. S., about the origin of which many guesses have been made, and 'bogus' derivations circumstantially given. Dr. S. Mr. Eber D. Howe, who was then editor of that paper, describes in his Autobiography (1878) the discovery of such a piece of mechanism in the hands of a gang of coiners at Painesville, in May 1827; it was a mysterious-looking object, and some one in the crowd styled it a 'bogus', a designation adopted in the succeeding numbers of the paper. Dr. Willard considers this to have been short for tantrabogus, a word familiar to him from his childhood, and which in his father's time was commonly applied in Vermont to any ill-looking object; he points out that tantarabobs is given in Halliwell as a Devonshire word for the devil. BOGUS seems thus to be related to BOGY, etc.] ... Bogus (bōu·gəs), sb.2 U. S. [Has been conjectured to be ad.
